newsitem.title: THAILAND: Thailand says offshore lending curbs won't hurt.
newsitem.headline: Thailand says offshore lending curbs won't hurt.

text.p: Further restrictions on offshore borrowing through the Bangkok International Banking Facility (BIBF) will not affect productive economic activity, a senior bank of Thailand official said on Thursday.

"Every time (we introduce measures) we will give protection to productive sectors of the economy," Nongnart Sondysuwan, deputy director of the financial institutions supervision and development department, told Reuters.
Last week the central bank decided to postpone proposed curbs aimed at further restricting loans originating from the offshore market.

The measures, aimed at curbing short-term foreign fund inflows into Thailand, alarmed BIBF lenders and sparked a sell- off in the equity market as investors factored in rising costs of funds for Thai corporates.
Earlier this year the Bank of Thailand (BOT), concerned by the country's growing exposure to foreign short term debt, introduced preliminary measures aimed at curbing loan growth.

Nongnart said a more detailed system of monitoring and reporting lending through the offshore facility should be in place next month. The results will help the BOT set up new restrictions targetted at borrowing for non-productive speculation.

"We will look at types of businesses. They might include speculation on securities, or real estate or comsumption sectors. We are quite concerned companies like this should depend on their own pockets," she said.
She said fears among foreign banks operating in the BIBF that the market would be too competitive to offer reasonable returns were unfounded.

"I think there is still profit to be made as pure BIBF lenders because the spread is quite clearly okay." She said offshore lenders could not expect to see returns matching those of the economic boom years.
This year Thai economic growth is forecast by private analysts to slow to around 7.0 percent, down from 8.6 percent gross domestic product aPLGDP growth in 1995.
Some foreign banks have hinted the slowdown, coupled with more restrictions, could force them to refocus their operations to Singapore.
Kobsak Duangdee, vice president of the Bank of Nova Scotia, said: "If conditions in the market are negative it will cause difficulty ... We have an office in Singapore, it depends on policies."

"You just can't tell customers you can't lend to them because of restrictions so you do the business out of Singapore," said Development Bank of Singapore country manager Ong Yeng Fang. "It's definitely more difficult this year and it has slowed a little, but I think that has more to do with the economic slowdown than with restrictions."

Nongnart said foreign banks were overcoming their initial reluctance to adapt to restrictions which cost them money in the short term, and were beginning to understand the measures are for the benefit of all parties in the longer term.
